notes.meaning: Jesus arrived in the village of Bethany just six days before the Passover celebration began. This was the hometown of Lazarus, whom Jesus had recently raised from the dead. Jesus knew that suffering waited for Him in nearby Jerusalem, yet He walked toward His final week willingly.

A dinner was held in Bethany to honor Jesus and celebrate Lazarus being alive. Martha showed her gratitude by serving the meal, while Lazarus reclined at the table with Jesus as living proof of His power over death. Both active service and quiet fellowship are genuine ways to honor the Lord.

Mary brought a jar of pure nard, a very rare and costly perfume imported from India. She poured it over Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair, showing extraordinary humility and love. The sweet scent filled the entire house, making her quiet sacrifice obvious to everyone present.

differ.view: Baptists understand Mary of Bethany to be a completely different person from Mary Magdalene and the unnamed repentant woman in Luke 7.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Western Catholic tradition historically identified Mary of Bethany, Mary Magdalene, and the sinful woman of Luke 7 as the same woman.

notes.meaning: Judas Iscariot quickly spoke up to object to Mary's loving gift. The writer reminds us here that Judas was the disciple who would soon betray Jesus to His enemies. His complaint did not come from love for God, but from an insincere and selfish heart.

Judas argued that the perfume should have been sold for three hundred silver coins, which was equal to a full year of a worker's wages. He claimed that this money could have been distributed to poor people. He used a good cause as a cover to hide his selfish complaints.

Judas did not actually care about the poor at all. He was the treasurer for Jesus and the disciples, and he had been secretly stealing money out of their shared bag. Greed had gained such control over his heart that he resented any gift given directly to Jesus.

Jesus told Judas to leave Mary alone and defended what she had done. He explained that her anointing prepared His body for the grave, pointing ahead to His coming death. God used her lavish devotion to mark Jesus out for His burial beforehand.

Jesus reminded His disciples that poor people would always be around them, giving them lifelong opportunities to show charity. But He would only be with them in person for a few more days. Loving and honoring Christ while He stood right before them was a unique, urgent moment.

A large crowd in nearby Jerusalem discovered where Jesus was staying and traveled out to Bethany. They came eager to see Jesus, but they also wanted to look at Lazarus with their own eyes. Seeing a man who had walked out of the grave stirred immense curiosity.

The leading priests were so troubled by the crowds that they began plotting to murder Lazarus as well. Lazarus had committed no crime, but his living presence proved Jesus' power in a way they could not deny. Blind hatred of the truth can drive people toward terrible cruelty.

Many people were turning away from the religious leaders and placing their faith in Jesus because of Lazarus. His restored life was a living witness that Jesus was truly the promised Messiah. The rulers feared losing their authority as the crowd's belief in Jesus grew.

The next day, the massive crowds visiting Jerusalem for the Passover festival heard that Jesus was on His way to the city. Many of these travelers had journeyed from Galilee and were eager to see Him. Joy and anticipation swept through the gathering pilgrims.

The people cut palm branches, which were traditional Jewish symbols of victory and royalty, and went out to welcome Jesus. They shouted words from Psalm 118, calling out 'Hosanna,' which means 'save now,' and hailed Him as Israel's King. They expected Him to be the great deliverer sent by God.

Jesus chose to ride into Jerusalem on a young donkey rather than on a military warhorse. This deliberate action fulfilled Old Testament prophecy and set the tone for His arrival. He presented Himself not as a violent soldier, but as a peaceful King.

This quotation from Zechariah told the people of Jerusalem not to fear their arriving King. A donkey was an animal of peace, showing that Jesus came to bring salvation rather than terror or war. Christ rules over His people with gentle grace.

The disciples did not understand the deep biblical meaning of these events while they were happening. It was only after Jesus rose from the dead, returned to heaven, and poured out the Holy Spirit that the scriptures made sense to them. God often gives us full understanding of His plans after we look back in faith.

Those who had stood by the tomb when Jesus called Lazarus back from the dead kept sharing what they had seen. They gave clear, eyewitness accounts of the miracle to the crowds arriving in Jerusalem. Their truthful testimony helped spread faith in Jesus throughout the city.

The crowd rushed out to meet Jesus largely because news of this mighty sign had reached them. Raising someone who had been buried for four days proved that Jesus possessed power over death itself. Real evidence of God's power naturally draws searching people to Jesus.

The Pharisees felt completely helpless as they watched the cheering crowds follow Jesus into the city. In their frustration, they complained to one another that none of their plots were working and that the whole world was running after Him. Without knowing it, they spoke words that pointed to the gospel reaching all nations.

A group of Greeks had traveled to Jerusalem to worship God during the Passover festival. These were Gentile believers who respected the God of Israel and came to pray at the temple courts. Their presence showed that people outside Israel were longing to know the true God.

These Greek visitors approached Philip with a respectful request to see Jesus. Philip had a Greek name and came from Galilee where Greeks lived, which likely made them feel comfortable asking him for help. They came with sincere hearts, desiring to learn from Jesus Himself.

Philip discussed the request with Andrew before taking it further, since bringing Gentiles to Jesus was unusual at the time. Together, both disciples went and told Jesus about the visitors. Working alongside other believers often helps us bring seekers to the Lord.

Jesus declared that the arrival of these Greek seekers meant the appointed time had finally arrived for Him to be glorified. Earlier He had said His hour had not yet come, but now His earthly work was nearing its peak. His true glory would be revealed through His death, resurrection, and ascension to heaven.

Jesus used an everyday picture from farming to explain why He had to die. A seed buried in the dirt looks like it is lost, but through that death it sprouts and produces a plentiful harvest of new wheat. In the same way, Jesus' death on the cross would yield the fruit of eternal life for countless believers.

Jesus explained that anyone who clings greedily to earthly life will end up losing it forever. But whoever values their earthly life lightly in comparison to following God will keep it for eternity. True, lasting life begins when we surrender our own desires to follow Christ.
